A commenter says the firm behind the offer is Slopfix, a software house focused entirely on refactoring AI-generated codebases. The pricing is outcome-based: the client pays in proportion to how much of [the reduction target] they hit.

The thread is mostly debate. Some commenters questioned the economics of a $10,000 engagement with three senior engineers for one week. Others pushed back on pricing by line count. The thread is about 104 days old, so the offer may have changed. I couldn't check the odra.dev page itself or confirm the price is still available.

The top result is a Hacker News thread about a codingwithjesse.com essay titled "Cleaning up after AI rockstar developers," posted about 132 days ago. The essay is only referenced by its title in the results, so I couldn't see its argument directly. The commenters mostly discuss the cleanup burden that AI-generated code creates for other developers.

- **Cleanup as a career path:** One commenter expects paid work fixing projects that coding agents leave behind, including bug fixes and migrations. (1-18, 1-19)
- **Workplace experience:** A developer says their senior colleagues now use AI for everything and hand the messy results to them to fix, which they find slow and thankless. (2-1, 2-4, 2-5, 2-13)
- **Pre-AI parallels:** Several commenters say the same problem existed with outsourced code and with long-time "rockstar" developers who left messes behind. (1-4, 1-28, 3-3)
- **Workflow debate:** Some argue that AI can handle much of its own cleanup through review loops, while others say that reverse-engineering design intent from rushed AI code is especially hard. (7-1, 1-77, 1-78)

Overall, the discussion treats cleanup as a substantial and possibly growing task, with views split on whether AI will reduce it over time.

I was wondering if vibe coding could...","url":"https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47387783"},{"title":"Vibe code is legacy code","url":"https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44739556"},{"title":"Ask HN: Any example of successful vibe-coded product?","url":"https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46434821"},{"title":"Will vibe coding end like the maker movement?","url":"https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47167931"},{"title":"Is Vibe Coding Dying?","url":"https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45842175"},{"title":"It's still ok to enjoy programming","url":"https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50134472"},{"title":"Gas Town's agent patterns, design bottlenecks, and vibecoding at scale","url":"https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46734302"},{"title":"Where Are the Vibecoded Photoshops?","url":"https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48177228"}]

The search turned up one main thread: a Hacker News discussion (item 47386636) of a blog post titled "The 100 hour gap between a vibecoded prototype and a working product" by macbudkowski.com. The post's text wasn't in the results, so what follows comes from the comments.

- **Speedup is modest for hard work:** One commenter estimated that for data pipelines, the LLM saves some time but nowhere near 10x, with the improvement dropping to about 2-3x because of back-and-forth review. Testing workloads that take hours to run still take hours to run with either a human or LLM testing them out.
- **The 80/20 split:** A widely shared argument holds that the LLM quickly produces the first 80%, but the remaining work barely shrinks, so a 100-hour job lands around 85 hours. This is at 1-36,1-37, 1-39,1-40.
- **Diagnosis:** One commenter attributed the gap to engineering knowledge, not vibecoding itself, arguing that most of the lost hours come from not noticing when the AI has gone off track. Another blamed the difference between writing code and architecting a product.
- **Real-world reports:** One builder said a prototype was basically working in one session, but roughly 30 more hours were needed before it felt ready. Another described a non-technical client's SaaS prototype that took about 200 hours and was unclear to clean up or secure.
- **Dissent:** Some commenters argued the gap is shrinking fast. One said the prototype-to-product time that took about six months in late 2024 was closer to two or three weeks by the time of the thread.

The thread is a community discussion, not a rigorous study, and the 100-hour figure is the blog author's own estimate.

Overall, the discussion suggests a real but unproven niche. Practitioners report taking on this work, while others question whether it's a standalone business.

Published figures for vibe coding cleanup work vary widely, and most come from vendors with something to sell.

- **Price range:** One cleanup-cost guide puts the spread at $299 for a freelance quick fix to $40,000 at the top of one company's band. The same author says most package prices fall between $1,500 and $8,000, though the spread mostly reflects how each seller scopes the job.
- **Freelancer rates:** Metana, a bootcamp provider, lists freelance rates at $100 to $300 per hour. A separate, self-described illustrative estimate of early-2026 platform rates suggests about $25–$60/hour for entry-level vibe coders and $60–$120/hour for mid-level practitioners, but it flags its own figures as unverified.
- **Platform averages:** One cleanup guide claims that on Upwork the average completed invoice for vibe code cleanup runs around $7,200. I could not verify that figure against another source.
- **Client volume:** In a 2025 report, freelancer Hamid Siddiqi said he regularly works with 15-20 clients and sometimes gets additional projects throughout the year.
- **Income:** Income claims are mostly marketing. One guide's example says a freelancer billing $150/hour working 20 billable hours per week makes $12,000/month, which assumes full utilization and steady demand.

I found no independent survey of actual cleanup freelancer earnings. The 404 Media piece that covers the trend is paywalled, and a LinkedIn screenshot of "cleanup specialists" that it mentions was not confirmed as genuine income.

- Core story: Freelancers and companies are building businesses around cleaning up after AI-generated code.
- Siddiqi: He has offered fixes on Fiverr for about two years, starting in late 2023, and says he handles roughly 15 to 20 regular clients plus one-off projects.
- Typical problems: Per Siddiqi, the recurring issues are inconsistent UI/UX, slow code, mismatched branding, and features that work but feel clunky. Siddiqi said the most common problems include inconsistent UI/UX, poorly optimized code that degrades performance, misaligned branding elements, and features that seem to work but feel clunky or unintuitive.
- Wider market: One report found that searching "vibe code fixer" on Fiverr returns over 230 results. It also cites Ulam Labs, which says on its website that "we clean up after vibe coding. Literally."
Sources secondhand to 404 Media.

Marketplace: VibeCodeFixers.com, founded by Swatantra Sohni, matches AI-built projects with developers. Founder says it has connected only 30-40 projects with experts so far.
